snippet:
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
Stephen Hubbard in the courtoomImage source, Reuters
Image caption,
Stephen Hubbard pictured in a Moscow courtroom as he was sentenced in 2024
ByMaia Davies
Published
21 October 2026, 10:22 BST
Updated 30 minutes ago
Russia has released a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for talks.
Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during the meeting early on Wednesday, according to Russian state media.
President Donald Trump later said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary".
Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024. He was accused of serving in a defence unit in Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.
Some other releases of detained Americans from Russia have been obtained through prisoner swaps.
Trump also appeared to defend his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force, writing that "if sanctions would have been placed", negotiations for Hubbard's release "would have come to a complete and total halt".
The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard, from Michigan, as "wrongfully detained" and the US president had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent.
"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused on Hubbard".
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

The head of the Australian federal police has condemned a “febrile” political environment that has seen one person charged every week over the alleged threatening of MPs, as Victoria announces new steps to protect politicians.
But the AFP and Victoria police insist they had no intelligence to suggest 43-year-old Brendan Nugent would go on to allegedly drive a Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP Helen Haines in a targeted attack.
Haines had one leg amputated after the alleged attack. Doctors had worked to save her second leg, but it was also amputated, her husband, Phil Haines, said at a press conference on Wednesday. Haines was in a stable condition, he said.
Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday morning on charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and a federal offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official, along with cannabis possession.

snippet:
Installing Python modules¶
As a popular open source development project, Python has an active supporting community of contributors and users that also make their software available for other Python developers to use under open-source license terms.
This allows Python users to share and collaborate effectively, benefiting from the solutions others have already created to common (and sometimes even rare!) problems, as well as potentially contributing their own solutions to the common pool.
This guide covers the installation part of the process. For a guide to creating and sharing your own Python projects, refer to the Python packaging user guide.
Note
For corporate and other institutional users, be aware that many organisations have their own policies around using and contributing to open source software. Please take such policies into account when making use of the distribution and installation tools provided with Python.
Key terms¶
pip is the preferred installer program. It is included by default with the Python binary installers.
A virtual environment is a semi-isolated Python environment that allows packages to be installed for use by a particular application, rather than being installed system wide.
venv is the standard tool for creating virtual environments. It defaults to installing pip into all created virtual environments.
virtualenv is a third-party alternative (and predecessor) to venv.
The Python Package Index (PyPI) is a public repository of open source licensed packages made available for use by other Python users.
The Python Packaging Authority is the group of developers and documentation authors responsible for the maintenance and evolution of the standard packaging tools and the associated metadata and file format standards. They maintain a variety of tools, documentation, and issue trackers on GitHub.

title: Beth Dobbin: British Olympic sprinter in bed for 22 hours a day after ME diagnosis - BBC Sport
snippet:
The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day
Figure caption,
'It feels like you're days away from death' - Beth Dobbin
ByKatie Falkingham
BBC Sport senior journalist
Published
16 October 2026
Beth Dobbin is so determined to raise awareness of the illness that has decimated her life that she is speaking out, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.
Five years ago, she ran for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics. Now, at 32, she spends more than 22 hours a day in bed.
"I've done little things like attend a blood test at the doctors and been in bed for months after. So doing this interview, chatting away for 30 minutes, that could have an impact on me in 2027," she says.
"But I felt like it was really important to do that to get the message out."
She now only gets out of bed to eat and use the bathroom.
Dobbin has been diagnosed with ME, or myalgic encephalomyelitis - a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more.
A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end.
This year, Dobbin has left the house on just five occasions.
"It's life-decimating like I can't even put into words," she says. "I feel like I've lost everything.
"I have still got my family, but I've lost my independence, my health, the ability to work, the ability to exercise."
For Dobbin it all started with back-to-back Covid and glandular fever infections in the winter of 2021-22. She had not been unwell with either, only discovering she had contracted both through retrospective tests.
She had been sleeping a bit more and her running times were slightly down, but nothing that raised alarm. As time went on, she noticed soreness in the glands of her neck and armpits and a general sense of not quite feeling herself.

Katie Boulter claimed a dominant win in her rain-affected first round match against Himeno Sakatsume in the Japan Open.
The British player was a set and 3-1 up against the home favourite when play was halted because of bad weather in Osaka on Monday.
She completed the win on Tuesday as she secured a 6-3 6-1 victory.
"Yesterday was a tough spot to end at," said Boulter, who will play Viktorija Golubic of Switzerland in the second round.
"I wanted to play last night and continue, but with the rain, unfortunately, that wasn't possible.
"It meant that I had to have the same mindset again today and just try to get over the line and focus on getting through the match.
"I think I did that. I didn't want to be out here playing a third set so I'm pleased with today."
Boulter, 30, took five of nine break points in the match and, even though she faced 13 break points, wildcard Sakatsume only managed to take one.
Elsewhere on Tuesday, Iga Swiatek elected to end her season before the WTA Finals in Indian Wells, with the world number nine and six-time Grand Slam winner withdrawing from the Ningbo Open because of a thigh injury and announcing her year on tour is over.

snippet:
Boulter wins in under an hour to reach quarters
Katie Boulter in a blue outfit and cap, with her racket held near her head after playing a shotImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Katie Boulter is British number two after Sonny Kartal replaced her at the top of the rankings on Monday
ByMike Peter
BBC Sport journalist
Published
4 hours ago
Katie Boulter moved into the quarter-finals of the Japan Open after she beat Viktorija Golubic in less than an hour.
The British number two defeated her Swiss opponent 6-2 6-1 in Osaka and will face either Croatia's Antonia Ruzic or American Kayla Day in the next round.
Boulter saved a break point in the opening game but dominated from 2-2 in the first set, winning nine games in a row before Golubic took the penultimate game of the match.
The 30-year-old lost the British number one spot to Sonny Kartal on Monday, but is set to retake the position following her run this week.
Boulter, who is seeded eighth in the competition, said she was pleased with how she handled "difficult conditions", with a strong wind affecting play.
"I think one of the biggest things for me is staying patient in the wind," she said.
"Sometimes I can get a little frustrated, and I'm very pleased that I didn't allow that to affect me today and I think I ended up playing some really good tennis in the second set. I'm really pleased with the performance."

snippet:
Dealing with Bugs¶
Python is a mature programming language which has established a reputation for stability. In order to maintain this reputation, the developers would like to know of any deficiencies you find in Python.
It can be sometimes faster to fix bugs yourself and contribute patches to Python as it streamlines the process and involves fewer people. Learn how to contribute.
Documentation bugs¶
If you find a bug in this documentation or would like to propose an improvement, please submit a bug report on the issue tracker. If you have a suggestion on how to fix it, include that as well.
You can also open a discussion item on our Documentation Discourse forum.
If you find a bug in the theme (HTML / CSS / JavaScript) of the documentation, please submit a bug report on the python-doc-theme issue tracker.

Using the Python issue tracker¶
Issue reports for Python itself should be submitted via the GitHub issues tracker (https://github.com/python/cpython/issues). The GitHub issues tracker offers a web form which allows pertinent information to be entered and submitted to the developers.
The first step in filing a report is to determine whether the problem has already been reported. The advantage in doing so, aside from saving the developers’ time, is that you learn what has been done to fix it; it may be that the problem has already been fixed for the next release, or additional information is needed (in which case you are welcome to provide it if you can!). History and License¶
History of the software¶
Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python’s principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.
In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see https://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software.
In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations, which became Zope Corporation. In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see https://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation was a sponsoring member of the PSF.

A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024.
The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second.
ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists.
The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them".
Data Cymru merged with the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) in 2025, who said there was no evidence the stolen information was "shared further or misused".
ONL and Data Cymru were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective.
During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families.

snippet:
How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?
An aerial view of the Jackdaw site inside a blue Verify frame
ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondendent
Published
28 minutes ago
The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.
BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.
Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?
Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.
The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external
Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Map showing the north of Scotland, the Orkney and Shetland Islands, the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. The Jackdaw gas field is marked on the map in the sea to the east of Aberdeen.
Where does Britain currently get its gas from?
Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.
Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.
But a higher share of the UK's gas imports now come in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) compared with 20 years ago.

title: South Africa vs Australia: Temba Bavuma century drags hosts back into series - BBC Sport
snippet:
Bavuma epic drags SA back into Test - have they time to beat Australia?
Temba Bavuma raises his bat after centuryImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Bavuma bettered his previous high score of 172
ByMatthew Henry
BBC Sport Journalist
Published
20 October 2026
Second Test, Gqeberha (day three of five)
South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81
Australia 3-1: Boland 2*; Rabada 1-0
Australia trail by 422 runs
Captain Temba Bavuma dragged South Africa back into their Test series against Australia with a masterful 179 on day three in Gqeberha.
Bavuma, who emerged in the gloom at 12-2 on day one, batted for 552 minutes across three days in making his highest Test score, allowing the Proteas to declare on 425-9 with half an hour to play having been 110-6 earlier on day three.
Kagiso Rabada nicked off Australia opener Nic Maddinson in the first over of Australia's reply to further boost the hosts' cause.
Bavuma's knock was every bit as impressive as Matthew Renshaw's 190 for Australia in their first Test win - arguably more so given the momentum that had built behind Australia since South Africa's batting struggles and the quality of the tourists' attack.
He remained composed in sharing partnerships of 132 with Marco Jansen and 183 with number nine Simon Harmer - the best eighth-wicket partnership in South Africa's Test history.
The century was Bavuma's fifth in Tests - 10 years after his first made him the first Black African to score a Test hundred for the Proteas.
He said it was "definitely" one of his best innings.
"That bowling attack, at least three are in the top 10 of the bowling rankings," he added. "There is a reason why."
More relevant for this series and England's tour to come over Christmas, it was Bavuma's fourth century in 14 Tests as South Africa captain.
He now averages 54.36 as Test skipper, compared with 34.53 across 93 innings before taking the reins. Few can match that improvement.

A teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.
The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.
Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.

title: Jackdaw: Will it cut energy bills and how much gas will it provide? - BBC News
snippet:
How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?
An aerial view of the Jackdaw site inside a blue Verify frame
ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondendent
Published
35 minutes ago
The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.
BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.
Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?
Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.
The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external
Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Map showing the north of Scotland, the Orkney and Shetland Islands, the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. The Jackdaw gas field is marked on the map in the sea to the east of Aberdeen.
Where does Britain currently get its gas from?
Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.
Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.
But a higher share of the UK's gas imports now come in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) compared with 20 years ago.

In keeping with its public service remit, and its obligations under the Disability Discrimination Act, the BBC will ensure that its media is accessible to people who have visual, hearing, motor or cognitive impairments.
Accessibility is a partnership between site producers like the BBC and the creators of the operating system, browser, and specialist assistive technologies which many disabled users employ to allow them, for example, to view websites in easier-to-read colours, with larger fonts, or as spoken text.

title: Woman told she had cancer by data-breaching hospital worker - BBC News
snippet:
Data-breach NHS worker told woman she had cancer
A woman in a brown cardigan and a silk scarf is looking intently into the camera with her hands clasped together. She is standing in front of green fields.
Image caption,
Pippa Boardman was told she had cancer by a hospital worker, days before her scheduled appointment with a consultant
By
South West health correspondent
Published
7 hours ago
A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.
Pippa Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said she had lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. She said she did not receive an apology from the hospital until it was contacted by the BBC.
The trust said it was "truly sorry" and "appropriate action had been taken".
It added: "While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously."
Boardman, who is now recovering well from cancer, said her personal information was accessed by a man she vaguely knew who worked at the hospital.
She said: "I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play.
"This man said to me 'Pippa, I don't want you to worry, but you've got cancer'.
"I just couldn't really believe it".
Two days later Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.
Nine months on, she said her strong recovery did not undo the damage done by the experience, adding: "I lost my dignity and I've lost my privacy."
Along with Boardman's case there have also been other recent NHS data breaches, described by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper as a disgrace.

Naomi ClarkeBBC Newsbeat

MNEK has cancelled his upcoming tour due to a lack of ticket sales and the show not being "ready to the standard" he wanted.
The Grammy-nominated artist, who has worked with the likes of Beyoncé, Zara Larsson and Madonna, was due to start a run of shows for his latest album Bulldozer!! next month.
In a statement shared on Instagram, the 31-year-old said he joins other artists who have cancelled shows recently as a result of "high production costs" and "over-ambitious planning".
Earlier this year, The Pussycat Dolls called off almost the entire US leg of their reunion tour following poor ticket sales.
The singer, whose real name is Uzoechi Emenike, said he had been "really looking forward" to performing his new album but had "no interest in doing this tour if I can't do it right".
He thanked fans who had bought tickets and said they would be refunded soon.
The artist also said he would try to tour the album when he could put on a show which fans "deserve".
Pop star Larsson, whose hit album Midnight Sun was executive produced by MNEK, was among those who offered their support to the artist in the comments.
Little Mix star Leigh-Anne Pinnock also sent him love, while singer Becky Hill encouraged him, saying: "Touring is devastatingly expensive but you'll find a way".

Sixty years on, the tragedy remains woven into the nation's collective memory, a day of unimaginable loss that reshaped a community and changed attitudes to industrial safety across Britain.

title: Missing German WW2 U-boat discovered off Devon 82 years on - BBC News
snippet:
Missing German WW2 U-boat found 82 years on
An underwater view of a submarine wreck, with fish swimming around it.Image source, Gasperados
Image caption,
The U-boat was scuttled by its own crew after it was attacked by the Royal Navy in July 1944
ByJohnny Rutherford and Britta ZeltmannDevon
Published
6 hours ago
A German submarine that went missing during World War Two after being damaged by the Royal Navy has been discovered 82 years on.
Plymouth dive team Gasperados identified the U-672 about 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe, Devon, after it was discovered by a deep sea diving team from Portland in August at a depth of about 230ft (70m).
The vessel was attacked by HMS Balfour in July 1944 but was scuttled by its 52 crew - all of whom survived. A navy log showing the sinking had incorrect coordinates, resulting in it not being found until recently.
Members of Gasperados said they were "really pleased" they could help identify the vessel.
Gasperados diver Dominic Robinson said: "Once we started moving around it and I started seeing the individual features - I saw the snorkel, I saw the conning tower, all those kind of things - I knew that we were going to get the video needed to identify it, so I was really pleased about that."
After its attack, the U-boat was left leaking underwater.
Its commander waited for as long as possible before making the decision to blow the tanks and bring the sub up to give its crew a last chance of survival.
Robinson said they "managed to get it to the surface" before getting into their life rafts for survival.
"They were bobbing around in the sea and then the very next day they were found by British aircraft, British vessels and then taken away to the prisoner of war camp," he explained.

title: Formula 1: Races to return to standard distance in 2028 - BBC Sport
snippet:
F1 races to return to standard distance in 2028
Formula 1 cars at the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand PrixImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
The maximum distance of a Formula 1 race will be reduced by 15km in 2027
By
F1 correspondent
Published
21 minutes ago
Formula 1 grands prix will return to their standard distance in 2028 after the maximum length was shortened for next season.
The maximum distance of a race was cut by 15km from 305km (189.5 miles) to 290km (180.2 miles) for the 2027 season.
That reduction was introduced because of a quirk of the situation surrounding changes to the engine rules for next year.
The new hybrid engines introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have been criticised for reducing the impact of driver skill.
The power split will be changed, in two steps, to 60-40 by 2028, enabling drivers to have maximum power for longer.
This means the cars will use more fuel - and that became a concern when it emerged some teams wanted to carry their chassis over into next year to save money.
As the fuel tank is within the chassis and therefore its size could not be changed, this meant those teams might not have been able to finish grands prix with their existing fuel tanks.
The change affects only a handful of races where fuel consumption is heaviest.
The sport's governing body, the FIA, published the 2027 rules this week and these included a section on changes for 2028 in which there is a clause that removes the reduction and reinstates the 305km maximum distance.

snippet:
Allen reveals mental health clinic stay before return
Mark AllenImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Allen returned to snooker after a five-month absence on Tuesday
ByMatt Gault
BBC Sport NI senior journalist
Published
1 hour ago
Mark Allen says he is working to "turn things around" and revealed he spent time in a mental health clinic before returning to snooker.
The former world number one lost to friend Jordan Brown in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open on Tuesday after five months away from the sport.
Speaking after the match, an emotional Allen said he was in a "bad place at the minute" and considering retirement.
"Everything I said in that interview was true. However, rest assured I'm doing my best to turn things round," Northern Ireland's Allen said in a statement on X on Wednesday.
He said he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic and discharged himself so he could prepare for Tuesday's match against Brown, adding that he plans to continue his treatment.
"I owed that to my family, in particular my daughter, to see me play for what could be the last time. I also owed it to the fans who have supported me throughout my 21 years on tour," added the 40-year-old.
"I also owed that to World Snooker who have been amazing from day one in all this, in particular Simon Brownell [CEO] and Neil Tomkins [World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association COO] who have remained in touch regularly, even Simon paying me a visit in the clinic itself."
The World Snooker Tour (WST) said they and the WPBSA are "supporting Mark and wish to help in any way we can".

Tighter rules planned to protect people from cosmetic surgery that goes badly wrong
13 hours ago
Michelle RobertsDigital health editor
FAMILY HANDOUT In this photo, Alice smiles at the camera and is sat in a barFAMILY HANDOUT
Alice Webb died after becoming unwell following a liquid Brazilian Butt Lift procedure
Only properly trained professionals will be allowed to offer high-risk cosmetic procedures like liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), vampire facials and chemical peels, under long-awaited government plans for England in 2027.
The government said it wanted to "drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market" and shield people from treatments "that can go badly wrong".
Currently, there are no restrictions over who can carry out these 'no scalpel' procedures, which can harm or kill if not performed safely.
Under the new rules, high-risk procedures for under-18s will also be banned, and rogue providers will face new criminal offences and fixed fines of up to £4,000.

Women have told the BBC of dangerous complications, pain and permanent scarring after treatment by rogue operators.

Python built-ins reference¶
Python comes with a number of built-in functions and classes.
The built-in classes include data types that would normally be considered part of the “core” of a language, such as numbers and lists. For these types, the Python language core defines the form of literals and places some constraints on their semantics, but does not fully define the semantics.
The built-ins also include functions and exceptions — objects that can be used by all Python code without the need of an import statement. Some of these are defined by the core language, but many are not essential for the core semantics and are only described here.
See also
In addition to the built-ins, Python provides an extensive importable standard library, see The Python standard library.

Missing German WW2 U-boat found 82 years on
An underwater view of a submarine wreck, with fish swimming around it.Image source, Gasperados
Image caption,
The U-boat was scuttled by its own crew after it was attacked by the Royal Navy in July 1944
ByJohnny Rutherford and Britta ZeltmannDevon
Published
7 hours ago
A German submarine that went missing during World War Two after being damaged by the Royal Navy has been discovered 82 years on.
Plymouth dive team Gasperados identified the U-672 about 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe, Devon, after it was discovered by a deep sea diving team from Portland in August at a depth of about 230ft (70m).
The vessel was attacked by HMS Balfour in July 1944 but was scuttled by its 52 crew - all of whom survived. A navy log showing the sinking had incorrect coordinates, resulting in it not being found until recently.
Members of Gasperados said they were "really pleased" they could help identify the vessel.
Gasperados diver Dominic Robinson said: "Once we started moving around it and I started seeing the individual features - I saw the snorkel, I saw the conning tower, all those kind of things - I knew that we were going to get the video needed to identify it, so I was really pleased about that."
After its attack, the U-boat was left leaking underwater.
Its commander waited for as long as possible before making the decision to blow the tanks and bring the sub up to give its crew a last chance of survival.
Robinson said they "managed to get it to the surface" before getting into their life rafts for survival.
"They were bobbing around in the sea and then the very next day they were found by British aircraft, British vessels and then taken away to the prisoner of war camp," he explained.

Billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Jio launches India's biggest share sale
7 hours ago
Rachita PrasadBBC News, Mumbai
LightRocket via Getty Images A security guard talks on his phone standing next to the logo of Jio on the wall.LightRocket via Getty Images
The Jio Platforms IPO is expected to be the biggest in the country
India's second richest man Mukesh Ambani's digital and telecommunications venture is tapping public investors for the first time in what's expected to be the country's largest share sale.
Jio Platforms, a unit of conglomerate Reliance Industries Ltd, aims to raise 302bn rupees ($3.2bn; £2.8bn) in the initial public offering (IPO) of freshly issued shares from Wednesday.
The company will use the money to repay loans it took to build and expand its unit Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd, India's largest private-sector telecoms operator.
This is the second mega IPO in a month in India after the National Stock Exchange's $2.4bn-issue despite the weakness in the broader equity market.
Arun Kejriwal of Kejriwal Research and Investment Services told the BBC that while the share market has remained subdued, the IPO market has been flush with issues and has seen interest from institutions and retail investors driven by attractive valuations and interest in new and scalable technology businesses.
He said that IPOs are being priced to reflect lower valuations and price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios among listed companies, making them attractive. The P/E ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay for each unit of a company's earnings.
Jio Platforms is offering shares in the price band of 1,065 to 1,119 rupees in the issue that closes Friday.
The share issue comes as the Nifty 50, the NSE's benchmark index of 50 leading Indian companies, has fallen by over 12% this year.
According to a Reuters report, institutional investors on Monday placed bids worth $3.2bn, which is 30 times the shares exclusively reserved for them and offered ahead of the IPO opening.

ByPaul Glynn
Culture reporter
Published

Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven".
West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North.
The award will go to the person who submits the funniest 1,000-word piece of first-person writing.
Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up."
The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North.
Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996.
It spawned several sequels and hit movie adaptations starring Renée Zellweger as the endearingly chaotic and lovelorn thirty-something diarist.
'Comedy heart'
In a statement announcing the prize, external, Fielding noted how the "comedy heart" of Bridget's story came from the "everyday humour of people around me when growing up in Yorkshire: laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth".

It is the sight no-one has seen for a generation.
Diggers in front of Lord's famous old pavilion. A gaping hole in the middle of the square.
After years of issues and complaints around the playing surface at cricket's spiritual home, those in charge have taken the drastic step to dig up one of its strips.
So what caused it, what is being done and what does it mean for the future?
What has caused the change?
The strip in question is Pitch Nine.
Lord's has 20 across the square but nine is one of five central strips used for the most high-profile matches.
Crucially, it was the controversial surface used for England's Test against New Zealand in June - a surface that proved incredibly difficult for batting.
Jacob Bethell was bowled by a ball that shot along the ground and the Test would have been over inside two days had it not been for bad weather.
Afterwards, England captain Ben Stokes said the surface does not benefit Test cricket and it was rated as "unsatisfactory" by the International Cricket Council.
Cricket's most historic venue had to deal with the ignominy of a demerit point being placed on its record.
What is being done?
The New Zealand Test was not the first case of Lord's - which is effectively guaranteed at least two Tests per year by the England and Wales Cricket Board - having trouble with its playing surface.
The pitches used for the men's Tests against Ireland in 2019, New Zealand in 2021 and Australia in 2023, plus a women's one-day international against India in 2022, were all rated "average" under the ICC's previous system.

snippet:
Extending and Embedding the Python Interpreter¶
This document describes how to write modules in C or C++ to extend the Python interpreter with new modules. Those modules can do what Python code does – define functions, object types and methods – but also interact with native libraries or achieve better performance by avoiding the overhead of an interpreter. The document also describes how to embed the Python interpreter in another application, for use as an extension language. Finally, it shows how to compile and link extension modules so that they can be loaded dynamically (at run time) into the interpreter, if the underlying operating system supports this feature.
This document assumes basic knowledge about C and Python. For an informal introduction to Python, see The Python Tutorial. The Python Language Reference gives a more formal definition of the language. Python built-ins reference documents the built-in functions and object types, and The Python standard library documents the modules (both built-in and written in Python) that give the language its wide application range.
For a detailed description of the whole Python/C API, see the separate Python/C API reference manual.
To support extensions, Python’s C API (Application Programmers Interface) defines a set of functions, macros and variables that provide access to most aspects of the Python run-time system. The Python API is incorporated in a C source file by including the header "Python.h".
Note
The C extension interface is specific to CPython, and extension modules do not work on other Python implementations. In many cases, it is possible to avoid writing C extensions and preserve portability to other implementations. History and License¶
History of the software¶
Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python’s principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.
In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see https://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software.
In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations, which became Zope Corporation. In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see https://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property. Zope Corporation was a sponsoring member of the PSF.
All Python releases are Open Source (see https://opensource.org for the Open Source Definition). Historically, most, but not all, Python releases have also been GPL-compatible; the table below summarizes the various releases.

Richard Jackson with a beard and short hair wearing a navy blue hoodie with you are enough written on it in white. He has a neutral expression and there is a fence and foilage behind him.Image source, Maddie Birch-Jackson

Former civil servant Richard Jackson made headlines in 2008 when he left top secret files on a train
ByJennifer Meierhans
Published

Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide
It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.
He had left highly classified documents on the train.
The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.
Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath, speaking to Dr Sian Williams for BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.
Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university.
"We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career.
"My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility.
"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."
He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.
Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.

Katie Boulter in a blue outfit and cap, with her racket held near her head after playing a shotImage source, Getty Images

ByMike Peter
BBC Sport journalist
Published
3 hours ago
Katie Boulter moved into the quarter-finals of the Japan Open after she beat Viktorija Golubic in less than an hour.
The British number two defeated her Swiss opponent 6-2 6-1 in Osaka and will face either Croatia's Antonia Ruzic or American Kayla Day in the next round.
Boulter saved a break point in the opening game but dominated from 2-2 in the first set, winning nine games in a row before Golubic took the penultimate game of the match.
The 30-year-old lost the British number one spot to Sonny Kartal on Monday, but is set to retake the position following her run this week.
Boulter, who is seeded eighth in the competition, said she was pleased with how she handled "difficult conditions", with a strong wind affecting play.
"I think one of the biggest things for me is staying patient in the wind," she said.
"Sometimes I can get a little frustrated, and I'm very pleased that I didn't allow that to affect me today and I think I ended up playing some really good tennis in the second set. I'm really pleased with the performance."

The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for strong winds as Storm Austen is forecast to sweep across parts of the UK.
The warning - the second-highest tier that the Met Office issues - is valid for Cornwall and parts of west Devon from 03:00 until 10:00 BST on Friday.
Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are expected around exposed coasts, with 60-70mph gusts elsewhere.
Flying debris could lead to injuries or a danger to life, with the risk of power cuts and damage to buildings.
A broader yellow Met Office wind warning covers large swathes of southern England and south Wales with some travel disruption possible.
Southern and eastern Scotland is also covered by a Met Office yellow warning - this one for heavy rain which could bring the risk of flooding.
When will Storm Austen arrive?
Storm Austen - an area of low pressure - is currently developing in the Atlantic and will continue to deepen as it approaches the UK.
It will move close to south-west England on Thursday night with the strongest winds expected to arrive early on Friday morning.
The very windiest conditions are expected on coastal headlands in north and west Cornwall - exposed to the north-westerly gales - but gusts of up to 70mph could occur even in inland areas.

title: Animal rights group Peta asks Crystal Palace to retire bald eagle mascot - BBC Sport
snippet:
Crystal Palace urged to retire bald eagle mascot
A black bald eagle, with its wings spread, on the arm of its male handlerImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Crystal Palace were rebranded as the Eagles in the mid-1970s, having previously been known as the Glaziers
Published
4 hours ago
An animal rights group is urging Crystal Palace to retire their live bald eagle mascot with immediate effect, saying a "bright stadium filled with boisterous fans is no place for animals".
In a letter to Palace CEO Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) asked the Premier League club to stop using the eagle, named Phoenix, in pre-match displays at Selhurst Park and to never use live animal mascots again.
The London team, known as the Eagles since 1973, introduced a live eagle to matchdays in 2010. Kayla, who died in 2020, performed the role for 10 years and her replacement Phoenix made her debut against West Ham in August 2024.
Peta says birds can become "frightened, disoriented and panicked" in stadium environments, putting themselves and fans at risk.
Using them for displays and entertainment also denies the animals, who "would naturally avoid humans", the opportunity to engage with their natural instincts, leading to "frustration and stress", the group said.
The organisation has "detailed records" of incidents involving live mascots, including birds, being injured or killed in collisions with walls, windows and match balls, as well as a falcon embedding its talons in a spectator's scalp after landing on his head.
In 2017, a Charlton Athletic fan was found guilty of trying to punch Kayla the eagle at a League Cup fixture two years earlier.
"Many professional sports teams use only willing humans as mascots and the club already has Pete the Eagle to excite the crowd," said Dr Carys Bennett, Peta's senior corporate projects manager.

Data-breach NHS worker told woman she had cancer
A woman in a brown cardigan and a silk scarf is looking intently into the camera with her hands clasped together. She is standing in front of green fields.

Pippa Boardman was told she had cancer by a hospital worker, days before her scheduled appointment with a consultant
By
South West health correspondent
Published
6 hours ago
A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.
Pippa Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said she had lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. She said she did not receive an apology from the hospital until it was contacted by the BBC.
The trust said it was "truly sorry" and "appropriate action had been taken".
It added: "While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously."
Boardman, who is now recovering well from cancer, said her personal information was accessed by a man she vaguely knew who worked at the hospital.
She said: "I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play.
"This man said to me 'Pippa, I don't want you to worry, but you've got cancer'.
"I just couldn't really believe it".
Two days later Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.
Nine months on, she said her strong recovery did not undo the damage done by the experience, adding: "I lost my dignity and I've lost my privacy."
Along with Boardman's case there have also been other recent NHS data breaches, described by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper as a disgrace.

An aerial view of the Jackdaw site inside a blue Verify frame
ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondendent

The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.
BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.
Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?
Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.
The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external
Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.
Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.

title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
snippet:
Christina Applegate says she was wrongly diagnosed with MS
16 hours ago
Brandon Drenon
AFP Christina Applegate pictured wearing a black top and smiling towards the cameraAFP
Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."
The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.
"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.
In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.
During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.
"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.
"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (French: Bureau international des poids et mesures, BIPM) is an intergovernmental organisation (IGO), through which its 67 member-states act on measurement standards in areas such as chemistry, ionising radiation, physical metrology, as well as the International System of Units (SI) and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).[2][3] It is headquartered in the Pavillon de Breteuil in Saint-Cloud, near Paris, France. The organisation has been referred to as IBWM (from its name in English) in older literature.[note 1]
Function
The BIPM has the mandate to provide the basis for a single, coherent system of measurements throughout the world, traceable to the International System of Units (SI). This task takes many forms, from direct dissemination of units to coordination through international comparisons of national measurement standards (as in electricity and ionising radiation).[5]
Following consultation, a draft version of the BIPM Work Programme is presented at each meeting of the General Conference for consideration with the BIPM budget. The final programme of work is determined by the CIPM in accordance with the budget agreed to by the CGPM.[6][7]

title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
snippet:
Christina Applegate says she was wrongly diagnosed with MS
16 hours ago
Brandon Drenon
AFP Christina Applegate pictured wearing a black top and smiling towards the cameraAFP
Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."
The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.
"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.
In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.
During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.
"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.
"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?

Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".

Hongwu Emperor
The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured Nanjing in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. He died in 1398 and was succeeded by his grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who was overthrown in 1402 by Zhu Di, later known as the Yongle Emperor. (Full article...)

snippet:
Boulter wins in under an hour to reach quarters
Katie Boulter in a blue outfit and cap, with her racket held near her head after playing a shotImage source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Katie Boulter is British number two after Sonny Kartal replaced her at the top of the rankings on Monday
ByMike Peter
BBC Sport journalist
Published
4 hours ago
Katie Boulter moved into the quarter-finals of the Japan Open after she beat Viktorija Golubic in less than an hour.
The British number two defeated her Swiss opponent 6-2 6-1 in Osaka and will face either Croatia's Antonia Ruzic or American Kayla Day in the next round.
Boulter saved a break point in the opening game but dominated from 2-2 in the first set, winning nine games in a row before Golubic took the penultimate game of the match.
The 30-year-old lost the British number one spot to Sonny Kartal on Monday, but is set to retake the position following her run this week.
Boulter, who is seeded eighth in the competition, said she was pleased with how she handled "difficult conditions", with a strong wind affecting play.
"I think one of the biggest things for me is staying patient in the wind," she said.
"Sometimes I can get a little frustrated, and I'm very pleased that I didn't allow that to affect me today and I think I ended up playing some really good tennis in the second set. I'm really pleased with the performance."

title: Git
snippet:
About Git
Git is fast
Git was built to work on the Linux kernel, meaning that it was built to handle repositories with tens of millions of lines of code from the start. Speed and performance has always been a primary design goal of Git.
Git also stores repository history efficiently. As of 2025, the current version of the Linux kernel's source code is 1.7 GB. Git stores the full history of the Linux project (1.4 million commits) in only 5.5 GB.
Git is widely used
According to the 2022 Stack Overflow developer survey, 96% of professional developers use Git.
Git has a huge ecosystem of tools
The core Git project is just a command-line tool, but Git exploded in popularity in the early 2010s thanks to Git hosting services like GitLab, GitHub, and more.
Since Git was created, many GUIs, editor integrations, and command line tools have been built to make working with Git more convenient. Your favorite developer tools might already have a built-in Git integration.
Free and Open Source
Git is released under the GNU General Public License version 2.0, which is an open source license. The Git project chose to use GPLv2 to guarantee your freedom to share and change free software---to make sure the software is free for all its users.
However, we do restrict the use of the term "Git" and the logos to avoid confusion. Please see our trademark policy for details.

title: Jackdaw: Will it cut energy bills and how much gas will it provide? - BBC News
snippet:
How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?
An aerial view of the Jackdaw site inside a blue Verify frame
ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondendent
Published
35 minutes ago
The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.
BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.
Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?
Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.
The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external
Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Map showing the north of Scotland, the Orkney and Shetland Islands, the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. The Jackdaw gas field is marked on the map in the sea to the east of Aberdeen.
Where does Britain currently get its gas from?
Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.
Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.
But a higher share of the UK's gas imports now come in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) compared with 20 years ago.

Dealing with Bugs¶
Python is a mature programming language which has established a reputation for stability. In order to maintain this reputation, the developers would like to know of any deficiencies you find in Python.
It can be sometimes faster to fix bugs yourself and contribute patches to Python as it streamlines the process and involves fewer people. Learn how to contribute.
Documentation bugs¶
If you find a bug in this documentation or would like to propose an improvement, please submit a bug report on the issue tracker. If you have a suggestion on how to fix it, include that as well.
You can also open a discussion item on our Documentation Discourse forum.
If you find a bug in the theme (HTML / CSS / JavaScript) of the documentation, please submit a bug report on the python-doc-theme issue tracker.

A list of documentation bugs that have been submitted to the Python issue tracker.
Overview of the process involved in reporting an improvement on the tracker.
Comprehensive guide for individuals that are interested in contributing to Python documentation.

Using the Python issue tracker¶
Issue reports for Python itself should be submitted via the GitHub issues tracker (https://github.com/python/cpython/issues). The GitHub issues tracker offers a web form which allows pertinent information to be entered and submitted to the developers.
The first step in filing a report is to determine whether the problem has already been reported. The advantage in doing so, aside from saving the developers’ time, is that you learn what has been done to fix it; it may be that the problem has already been fixed for the next release, or additional information is needed (in which case you are welcome to provide it if you can!). Huge crowds watch attempt to save shark stranded in South Korean canal
Huge crowds have flocked to a canal in South Korea to watch a stranded shark.
The 9ft 10in (3m) shark, nicknamed Bukangi, was first spotted in the waterway last month in the south-eastern city of Busan.
Now a third attempt has been made to rescue the female using nets to guide her back to the open sea.
It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish.
The BBC's Seoul correspondent Jake Kwon goes to Busan to follow the latest attempt to rescue Bukangi.

A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal working fine go away.
Mohammad Alias Yousaf, also known as Alias, made the claim to an undercover reporter posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker. The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could get out of the fine - if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.
Alias has denied ever providing such advice, or giving false information to the Home Office.
In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way illegal working fines are issued and collected.
Our UK editor, Ed Thomas, reports.

title: Hackers steal children's data after company used 'Password1' for old account - BBC News
snippet:
Hackers steal children's data after company used 'Password1' to protect old account
A close-up of a woman's hand typing on a computer keyboard in the dark against colourful lights in background. The keyboard is lit up.Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Hackers stole information from Data Cymru's systems in 2024 which exposed the personal information of 3,300 people
ByAngharad Thomas
BBC Wales
Published
1 hour ago
A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said.
The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024.
The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second.
ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists.
The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them".
Data Cymru merged with the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) in 2025 and now follows WLGA data protection protocols, including the use of "strengthened" passwords.
The WLGA said there was no evidence the stolen information was "shared further or misused".
ONL and Data Cymru were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective.
During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families.

title: Installing Python modules — Python 3.15.0 documentation
snippet:
Installing Python modules¶
As a popular open source development project, Python has an active supporting community of contributors and users that also make their software available for other Python developers to use under open-source license terms.
This allows Python users to share and collaborate effectively, benefiting from the solutions others have already created to common (and sometimes even rare!) problems, as well as potentially contributing their own solutions to the common pool.
This guide covers the installation part of the process. For a guide to creating and sharing your own Python projects, refer to the Python packaging user guide.
Note
For corporate and other institutional users, be aware that many organisations have their own policies around using and contributing to open source software. Please take such policies into account when making use of the distribution and installation tools provided with Python.
Key terms¶
pip is the preferred installer program. It is included by default with the Python binary installers.
A virtual environment is a semi-isolated Python environment that allows packages to be installed for use by a particular application, rather than being installed system wide.
venv is the standard tool for creating virtual environments. It defaults to installing pip into all created virtual environments.
virtualenv is a third-party alternative (and predecessor) to venv.
The Python Package Index (PyPI) is a public repository of open source licensed packages made available for use by other Python users.
The Python Packaging Authority is the group of developers and documentation authors responsible for the maintenance and evolution of the standard packaging tools and the associated metadata and file format standards. They maintain a variety of tools, documentation, and issue trackers on GitHub.
Changed in version 3.5: The use of venv is now recommended for creating virtual environments.

The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. snippet:
http.cookies — HTTP state management¶
The http.cookies module defines classes for abstracting the concept of cookies, an HTTP state management mechanism. It supports both simple string-only cookies, and provides an abstraction for having any serializable data-type as cookie value.
The module formerly strictly applied the parsing rules described in the RFC 2109 and RFC 2068 specifications. It has since been discovered that MSIE 3.0x didn’t follow the character rules outlined in those specs; many current-day browsers and servers have also relaxed parsing rules when it comes to cookie handling. As a result, this module now uses parsing rules that are a bit less strict than they once were.
The character set, string.ascii_letters, string.digits and !#$%&'*+-.^_`|~: denote the set of valid characters allowed by this module in a cookie name (as key).
Changed in version 3.3: Allowed ‘:’ as a valid cookie name character.
Note
On encountering an invalid cookie, CookieError is raised, so if your cookie data comes from a browser you should always prepare for invalid data and catch CookieError on parsing.
exception http.cookies.CookieError¶
Exception failing because of RFC 2109 invalidity: incorrect attributes, incorrect Set-Cookie header, etc.

title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
snippet:
Christina Applegate says she was wrongly diagnosed with MS
16 hours ago
Brandon Drenon
AFP Christina Applegate pictured wearing a black top and smiling towards the cameraAFP
Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."
The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.
"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.
In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.
During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.
"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.
"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

He had left highly classified documents on the train.

"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."
He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.
Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.
Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".

snippet:
Extending and Embedding the Python Interpreter¶
This document describes how to write modules in C or C++ to extend the Python interpreter with new modules. Those modules can do what Python code does – define functions, object types and methods – but also interact with native libraries or achieve better performance by avoiding the overhead of an interpreter. The document also describes how to embed the Python interpreter in another application, for use as an extension language. Finally, it shows how to compile and link extension modules so that they can be loaded dynamically (at run time) into the interpreter, if the underlying operating system supports this feature.
This document assumes basic knowledge about C and Python. For an informal introduction to Python, see The Python Tutorial. The Python Language Reference gives a more formal definition of the language. Python built-ins reference documents the built-in functions and object types, and The Python standard library documents the modules (both built-in and written in Python) that give the language its wide application range.
For a detailed description of the whole Python/C API, see the separate Python/C API reference manual.
To support extensions, Python’s C API (Application Programmers Interface) defines a set of functions, macros and variables that provide access to most aspects of the Python run-time system. The Python API is incorporated in a C source file by including the header "Python.h".

title: Embedding Python in Another Application — Python 3.15.0 documentation
snippet:
Embedding Python in Another Application¶
The previous chapters discussed how to extend Python, that is, how to extend the functionality of Python by attaching a library of C functions to it. It is also possible to do it the other way around: enrich your C/C++ application by embedding Python in it. Embedding provides your application with the ability to implement some of the functionality of your application in Python rather than C or C++. This can be used for many purposes; one example would be to allow users to tailor the application to their needs by writing some scripts in Python. You can also use it yourself if some of the functionality can be written in Python more easily.
Embedding Python is similar to extending it, but not quite. The difference is that when you extend Python, the main program of the application is still the Python interpreter, while if you embed Python, the main program may have nothing to do with Python — instead, some parts of the application occasionally call the Python interpreter to run some Python code.
So if you are embedding Python, you are providing your own main program. One of the things this main program has to do is initialize the Python interpreter. At the very least, you have to call the function Py_Initialize(). There are optional calls to pass command line arguments to Python. Then later you can call the interpreter from any part of the application.
There are several different ways to call the interpreter: you can pass a string containing Python statements to PyRun_SimpleString(), or you can pass a stdio file pointer and a file name (for identification in error messages only) to PyRun_SimpleFile(). You can also call the lower-level operations described in the previous chapters to construct and use Python objects.

The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for strong winds as Storm Austen is forecast to sweep across parts of the UK.
The warning - the second-highest tier that the Met Office issues - is valid for Cornwall and parts of west Devon from 03:00 until 10:00 BST on Friday.
Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are expected around exposed coasts, with 60-70mph gusts elsewhere.

Southern and eastern Scotland is also covered by a Met Office yellow warning - this one for heavy rain which could bring the risk of flooding.

It will move close to south-west England on Thursday night with the strongest winds expected to arrive early on Friday morning.
The very windiest conditions are expected on coastal headlands in north and west Cornwall - exposed to the north-westerly gales - but gusts of up to 70mph could occur even in inland areas.

title: Python built-ins reference — Python 3.15.0 documentation
snippet:
Python built-ins reference¶
Python comes with a number of built-in functions and classes.
The built-in classes include data types that would normally be considered part of the “core” of a language, such as numbers and lists. For these types, the Python language core defines the form of literals and places some constraints on their semantics, but does not fully define the semantics.
The built-ins also include functions and exceptions — objects that can be used by all Python code without the need of an import statement. Some of these are defined by the core language, but many are not essential for the core semantics and are only described here.
See also
In addition to the built-ins, Python provides an extensive importable standard library, see The Python standard library.

snippet:
What’s new in Python 3.15¶
Editor:
Hugo van Kemenade
This article explains the new features in Python 3.15, compared to 3.14. Python 3.15 was released on 9 October 2026. For full details, see the changelog.
See also
PEP 790 – Python 3.15 release schedule
Summary – Release highlights¶
Python 3.15 is the latest stable release of the Python programming language, with a mix of changes to the language, the implementation, and the standard library. The biggest changes include lazy imports, frozendict and sentinel builtins, UTF-8 as the default encoding, unpacking in comprehensions, and a stable ABI for free-threaded builds.
The library changes include a new profiling package with Tachyon, a high-frequency statistical sampling profiler, more color in command-line output, as well as the usual deprecations and removals, and improvements in user-friendliness and correctness.
This article doesn’t attempt to provide a complete specification of all new features, but instead gives a convenient overview. For full details refer to the documentation, such as the Library Reference and Language Reference. To understand the complete implementation and design rationale for a change, refer to the PEP for a particular new feature; but note that PEPs usually are not kept up-to-date once a feature has been fully implemented.

Published
